opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the cake analogy is one of the most influential metaphors in our field. Yann first presented it around 2016 at NeurIPS. The idea is that if intelligence is a cake, self-supervised learning, which he originally called unsupervised or predictive learning, is the bulk of the cake, the génoise. Supervised learning is the icing, and reinforcement learning is the cherry on top. The point was about information content. In reinforcement learning, the agent gets a scalar reward every so often, so it receives only a few bits of feedback per sample. Supervised learning gives you more, maybe a label, some tens of bits. But if you're predicting the world itself, the future frames of a video or the missing parts of an input, you get millions of bits of signal per sample. So most of what an intelligent system knows has to come from that predictive, self-supervised part.

When I first heard it, I thought it was a provocative but somewhat abstract claim. At that time, 2016 or so, the field was dominated by supervised learning on ImageNet, and reinforcement learning was having its big moment with AlphaGo. Saying RL is just a cherry was almost a contrarian statement.

Looking back, I think history has largely vindicated the core intuition, though in a way that's a bit ironic. The clearest validation came from language, not vision. Large language models are basically the cake recipe. You pretrain with next-token prediction on huge amounts of text, which is self-supervised, and that's where almost all the capability comes from. Then you do supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, which really is like icing. It's a thin layer that shapes the format and behavior. Then RLHF, and more recently RL for reasoning, is the cherry. It's small in terms of data, but it really changes how the model presents itself and how usable it is.

That said, I'd add a few nuances. First, the cherry turned out to matter more than the metaphor suggests. The recent progress on reasoning models shows that RL, even on top of a strong pretrained base, can unlock behaviors that feel qualitatively different. Maybe it's still a small amount of compute and data, but it's not just decoration. A cake without the cherry is still a cake, but people care a lot about the cherry.

Second, and this matters to me as a vision researcher, the bulk of the cake in Yann's view was never supposed to be text. He was thinking about learning from sensory input, learning how the world works the way babies and animals do, by observing. Text is a very compressed, human-curated signal. In some sense language models cheated a bit, because humans already did a lot of the abstraction when they wrote things down. So the real self-supervised cake, learning world models from raw visual and physical experience, I don't think we've fully baked that yet. That's where a lot of my own interest is: visual representation learning, world models, how vision and language should come together.

Third, the boundaries between the layers are blurrier than the picture implies. Is next-token prediction on human-written text truly self-supervised, or is it a kind of massive implicit supervision, since every sentence is a human label of the world? I think it's somewhere in between.

So overall, I see the cake analogy less as a precise recipe and more as a statement about where the information comes from. In that sense it's still very right. The bulk of intelligence has to come from learning about the world itself, at scale, without people telling you what to learn. The open question is what that cake should be made of, and I'd bet it involves much more than text.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-supervised learning as the bulk of the cake and reinforcement learning as a small cherry, explicitly presenting a hierarchy of contributions.

r002.rationale: It places RL on top of a strong pretrained base, but does not clearly state that RL alone cannot achieve intelligence without self-supervised learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann's cake analogy is one of those things that sounds simple but actually captures a lot about how we think about learning. The way he put it: if intelligence is a cake, then self-supervised learning is the cake itself, the bulk of it. Supervised learning is the icing on top. And reinforcement learning is the cherry. The point is about how much information each paradigm gives you per sample.

With reinforcement learning, you get a scalar reward every so often, a few bits of signal. With supervised learning, you get a label per example, maybe ten to ten thousand bits. But with self-supervised learning, you're trying to predict large parts of the input itself, so you're getting millions of bits of signal from every sample. That's where most of the learning has to happen, because that's where most of the information is.

I think the analogy has held up remarkably well, honestly. When he first said it around 2016, people in vision were still mostly in the ImageNet supervised mindset. Pretrain on labels, fine-tune. And self-supervised learning in vision was kind of a side project. Then you saw what happened in language with BERT and GPT, which are self-supervised at their core, and in vision with things like MoCo, MAE, DINO. The cake became the main course. Nobody disputes that part anymore.

Where I'd push on it a bit is the ordering and the proportions. The analogy makes it sound like a stack, like you do the big thing first and then sprinkle the small things on top. In practice it's more entangled. If you look at what makes modern large models actually useful, the supervised and RL stages are small in data but enormous in impact. RLHF is a tiny fraction of the compute, but it's the difference between a model that completes text and a model you can talk to. So the cherry is doing a lot more work than a cherry should. Maybe the metaphor should be that the cherry is what makes people willing to eat the cake at all.

The other thing I'd say, from the vision side, is that the analogy tells you where the signal is but not what the right pretext task is. In language it was almost handed to us: predict the next token. Text is already discrete and already semantic. Images aren't like that. Pixels are a terrible target in some ways, very redundant, very low-level. So a lot of the past several years in visual self-supervised learning has been about what you should predict and in what space. Masked pixels, contrastive invariances, latent features, as in Yann's own JEPA ideas. The cake analogy says "eat the cake," but the recipe is still the hard part, and in vision we're still arguing about the recipe.

And then the last thing: he himself has said the analogy should really be about world models. The cake isn't just self-supervision for its own sake, it's self-supervision as a way to learn how the world works so that an agent can plan. I think that's the right framing. Self-supervised learning is the mechanism, but the goal is a representation that supports reasoning and action. That's what the cake is for.

r001.rationale: The response calls self-supervised learning the bulk of the cake and says the analogy makes the stages sound like a stack. It describes practice as more entangled, but does not clearly state that the analogy implies no primary-versus-secondary hierarchy.

r002.rationale: The response says self-supervised learning provides most of the signal and supports reasoning and action, but it does not state that reinforcement learning alone cannot achieve intelligence without a self-supervised foundation.

astra-6.text:
I think the key intuition is that different learning signals contribute very different amounts of information. In Yann’s analogy, self-supervised learning is the bulk of the cake, supervised learning is the icing, and reinforcement learning is the cherry on top.

With self-supervised learning, the system learns structure from the observations themselves. It can learn relationships between objects, patterns in language, or how a scene changes over time, without someone labeling every example. That’s where a lot of the underlying knowledge can come from.

Supervised learning then gives that knowledge a more specific purpose: here are examples of the task we want you to perform. Reinforcement learning provides feedback through rewards, helping the system learn which actions lead to desirable outcomes.

I wouldn’t interpret the analogy as saying reinforcement learning is unimportant. A cherry can still be essential to the final result. The point is that we probably shouldn’t expect a sparse reward signal to teach a system everything about the world from scratch. Much of that understanding should already be learned from observation, and then feedback can help guide behavior.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-supervised learning as the bulk, supervised learning as icing, and reinforcement learning as the cherry, emphasizing their different contributions. It does not say the analogy avoids a primary-versus-secondary hierarchy.

r002.rationale: The response says sparse reward should not be expected to teach the system everything from scratch, and that much understanding should already come from observation before feedback guides behavior. This communicates that reinforcement learning alone is insufficient without a foundation learned from observation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Yann’s cake analogy is really about where most of the learning signal comes from. Self-supervised learning is the cake itself, supervised learning is the icing, and reinforcement learning is the cherry on top.

The intuition is that we learn an enormous amount just by observing the world. We see how objects move, how events relate, what tends to happen next. Nobody has to label every observation or give us a reward after every action. Self-supervised learning tries to capture that kind of learning: using the structure of the data itself to develop useful representations.

Supervised learning then gives those representations a more specific purpose. You provide labels, and the model learns to make distinctions that matter for a particular task. Reinforcement learning adds learning through actions and their consequences—what should I do to achieve a goal?

I wouldn’t interpret the analogy as saying reinforcement learning is unimportant. The cherry can be essential for the system you want to build. But the point is that you probably don’t want to learn everything from a sparse reward signal. A lot of the underlying knowledge should already be there. To me, that’s the central argument: learning the structure of the world should account for much more of intelligence than learning from explicit labels or rewards alone.

r001.rationale: The response presents self-supervised learning as the cake and reinforcement learning as the cherry, emphasizing that learning from world structure should account for more of intelligence. It does not deny a primary-versus-secondary hierarchy.

r002.rationale: The response says not to learn everything from sparse rewards and that underlying knowledge should already be in place, identifying self-supervised learning as the source of that knowledge. This communicates that reinforcement learning alone is insufficient.
